beats.say: The Milwaukee police had Jeffrey Dahmer. Twice. And both times, they let him go.
Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Between nineteen seventy eight and nineteen ninety one, seventeen young men went missing from these streets.
Seventeen lives. Most of them young, Black or brown, and gay. Men whose disappearances drew almost no headlines at all.
And the killing was not steady. It accelerated. One victim in nineteen seventy eight. Four in nineteen ninety. Eight in the final seven months.

Here is what the system already knew. A nineteen eighty nine conviction for assaulting a child. A sentence served on work release. Probation, with required monthly check ins, running through the deadliest years.
Then came the night of May twenty seventh, nineteen ninety one. The night this should have ended.
A fourteen year old boy escaped the apartment and reached the street. Neighbours called nine one one, and stayed with him. Officers arrived, believed Dahmer's story, and walked the boy back inside.

visual.title: That night
steps: Neighbours call 911 and stay with him
Officers return him to the apartment

beats.say: The officers' own radio log survives. Listen to the words they chose.

visual.text: Intoxicated Asian, naked male, was returned to his sober boyfriend.

beats.say: Four more men died after that night. It ended only in July, when a survivor escaped and led police back to the apartment.

visual.headline: Suspect held as remains found in Oxford flats
visual.body: A 32-year-old chocolate factory worker was arrested late Monday after a man who escaped the apartment flagged a patrol car on North 25th Street. Investigators worked through the night.

beats.say: Sixteen life sentences followed. The officers who returned the boy were reinstated, with back pay. The neighbours who called nine one one were never once called to testify that night was preventable. The verdict was for one man. The questions were for the city.
